items.questionAndWhy: Do pessimism, optimism or biased judgments predict which conspiracy narratives people engage with online?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers linked measures of optimism, pessimism and judgment bias from 2,506 US Twitter users to more than 7.7 million social-media engagements, examining six COVID-19 conspiracy narratives.
items.whatTheyFound: Dispositional pessimism was associated with engagement in one system-blame narrative about corporations benefiting from the pandemic, but not the other five. Optimism and measured judgment bias predicted none of the six.
items.whatItMeans: A psychological disposition may matter for a specific narrative rather than for conspiracy engagement generally. These observational relationships do not show that pessimism causes belief or sharing.
items.streamTitle: Pessimism predicted engagement with only one of six conspiracy narratives
items.streamSummary: Among 2,506 Twitter users, pessimism related to engagement with one system-blame conspiracy narrative, not five others. Optimism and task-measured judgment bias showed no comparable links; causality was not tested.

items.questionAndWhy: Are beneficial urban soundscapes more than simply the absence of noise, and do effects depend on context?
items.whatTheyDid: A systematic review covered 194 studies; a meta-analysis combined 1,658 effect sizes from 66 studies covering 28 sound sources and different well-being outcomes.
items.whatTheyFound: Natural sounds had positive pooled effects across examined outcomes (Hedges' g roughly 0.53–0.59). Human sounds showed more selective, context-dependent benefits. Evidence for behavior and social well-being was thinner than for health.
items.whatItMeans: Urban planning should examine what people hear and how sounds fit the setting, not just noise levels. Variable study quality, settings and measures limit generalization.
items.streamTitle: Natural sounds showed more consistent well-being benefits than human sounds
items.streamSummary: A review of 194 studies and meta-analysis of 66 found fairly consistent positive associations for natural sounds; human sounds depended more on context. Behavioral and social outcomes were studied less often.
items.attribution: Guo et al. — npj Urban Sustainability (systematic review and meta-analysis)

items.questionAndWhy: Could consistently affirming AI tutors make learners less able to accept corrective feedback?
items.whatTheyDid: A conceptual Perspective defined critical-feedback tolerance, distinguished it from related constructs, and proposed measurable indicators and conditions that could refute the hypothesis.
items.whatTheyFound: The paper offers a testable framework, not an intervention result. It presents no new experiment demonstrating that AI agreement reduces feedback tolerance.
items.whatItMeans: AI-learning evaluations could test constructive disagreement and response to correction, not just user satisfaction. Any claimed psychological harm remains a hypothesis until tested.
items.streamTitle: Researchers proposed testing whether agreeable AI weakens tolerance for criticism
items.streamSummary: A new Perspective argues that overly agreeable AI may undermine learners' tolerance for corrective feedback. It defines ways to test the claim but reports no new empirical evidence of harm.
items.attribution: Chen et al. — npj Digital Medicine (Perspective)

items.questionAndWhy: Do AI tool-safety benchmarks measure genuine policy judgment or shortcuts in how test cases are formatted?
items.whatTheyDid: A preprint audited three released agent-safety datasets using simple label predictors, domain-held-out tests, different evaluation weights and paired wording/tool-name changes in a 64-step cohort.
items.whatTheyFound: Exact-tool label prediction fell from F1 0.901 to 0.495 on a new domain; a guard's reported F1 changed from 0.902 to 0.719 under equal-interaction weighting. Paired edits changed one model's blocking but did not reproduce similarly in another.
items.whatItMeans: Evaluate agents with domain holdouts, stable test units and controlled input perturbations. The results expose benchmark sensitivity, not proof that every guard or benchmark is invalid.
items.streamTitle: Safety benchmarks changed when superficial agent-context cues were altered
items.streamSummary: An arXiv audit found large shifts in agent-safety scores under domain holdouts and alternative weighting. Small input edits affected one tested guard but not all models, underscoring evaluation fragility.
items.attribution: Demirkiran and Ernstberger — arXiv preprint (Shortcut Sensitivity)

items.questionAndWhy: Can combining language, images and emotional signals improve classification of misleading crisis posts?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers combined XLM-R text representations, ViT image features, emotion and sentiment models, and a stacked classifier; they evaluated four existing datasets including a Ukraine-related set.
items.whatTheyFound: Reported accuracies were 94.66% on Fakeddit, 98.23% on Ukraine-GitHub, 98.12% on Weibo and 97.98% on MediaEval. These are retrospective dataset scores, not demonstrated detection during live conflicts.
items.whatItMeans: Multimodal ensembles may be useful for triage, but reliability claims need temporal and cross-event validation, transparent labeling standards and calibrated field tests.
items.streamTitle: Conflict-misinformation ensemble reported high scores on four benchmarks
items.streamSummary: An ensemble using text, imagery and affective features reported 94.66%–98.23% accuracy across four misinformation datasets. Results were benchmark-based and do not establish live conflict performance.

items.questionAndWhy: Can language models estimate changes in depression from very short, open-ended daily diaries?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers studied 108 participants, including people in treatment. They compared LLM ratings from 14–21 days of video-diary transcripts with daily questionnaires and baseline clinical interviews.
items.whatTheyFound: LLM ratings correlated with within-person self-reports (r=0.45), averaged self-reports (r=0.61) and interview-assessed symptom severity (r=0.53). These are associations, not diagnostic sensitivity or specificity.
items.whatItMeans: Narrative-based measurement may complement questionnaires, but clinical screening, fairness, privacy and prospective performance require separate validation.
items.streamTitle: Brief diaries gave AI a moderate signal of depression, not a diagnosis
items.streamSummary: In 108 participants, LLM depression scores from short diary transcripts moderately tracked surveys and clinical interviews. The study tested measurement validity, not diagnostic accuracy or patient outcomes.
items.attribution: Ringwald et al. — npj Digital Medicine

items.questionAndWhy: Are existing courtroom evidence rules sufficient as synthetic audio and video become harder to authenticate?
items.whatTheyDid: At an October 15 federal judicial advisory meeting, technology specialists presented concerns about synthetic media; the committee considered experiences reported in a survey of 931 federal judges and formed a subcommittee.
items.whatTheyFound: Only 15 surveyed judges reported a deepfake-related evidence challenge. Speakers warned that detection tools lack universal reliability, while some judges cautioned against premature special rules. No new rule was adopted.
items.whatItMeans: Evidence-authentication policy must weigh emerging technical risks against documented courtroom incidence. Neither industry forecasts nor low historical case counts settle future prevalence.
items.streamTitle: US evidence-rule advisers confronted deepfakes but reported few actual challenges
items.streamSummary: At an October 15 US judicial panel, experts warned of increasingly convincing deepfakes, while only 15 of 931 surveyed judges had seen related challenges. A subcommittee will study the issue; no rule was adopted.
items.attribution: Reuters — Nate Raymond, original reporting from US Judicial Conference meeting

items.questionAndWhy: Can event-level records reveal when disasters and public announcements are followed by surges in psychological-support demand?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers analyzed 138,471 Mexico City digital screening and crisis-support interactions from 2020–2023, comparing event dates, symptom patterns and service demand.
items.whatTheyFound: Different events coincided with short-run shifts in demand and symptoms. One reported day showed a 2,651% increase in interactions. The observational analyses cannot attribute these changes uniquely to specific announcements or hazards.
items.whatItMeans: Emergency services can use time-resolved demand data for staffing scenarios, while accounting for overlapping events, changing access and baseline variation before forecasting capacity.
items.streamTitle: Disaster-linked demand spikes may overwhelm remote mental-health support
items.streamSummary: Analysis of 138,471 Mexico City mental-health service interactions found sharp short-term demand changes near public-health and disaster events, including one 2,651% daily spike. The study is observational.
items.attribution: Garibay Rubio et al. — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

items.questionAndWhy: Can language-model summaries make preparation for a first oncology consultation easier in real clinical workflows?
items.whatTheyDid: Nine clinicians were assessed at baseline and then used AI-generated consultation preparation for 33 appointments in a prospective single-group pre/post usability study.
items.whatTheyFound: Clinicians reported 28.9% lower workload and 3.26 minutes saved per case. Preparation succeeded for 84.9% of consultations, but only 63.6% of summaries were complete. No randomized comparison established objective benefits.
items.whatItMeans: Usability gains can coexist with omitted information. Larger controlled studies should measure correctness, completeness, actual time saved and downstream care.
items.streamTitle: Oncology AI summaries reduced reported workload but remained incomplete
items.streamSummary: In a small oncology workflow study, clinicians reported lower workload and about three minutes saved per case, but only 63.6% of AI summaries were complete. Benefits remain exploratory.
items.attribution: van Koevorden et al. — npj Digital Medicine

items.questionAndWhy: How quickly do local economies recover after hurricanes, and what predicts disruption better than a storm's category?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers examined aggregated daily payment transactions in 7,987 US ZIP codes affected by 21 Atlantic hurricanes from 2017 through 2024, comparing merchant sales and customer spending patterns.
items.whatTheyFound: Hurricanes caused losses roughly equivalent to two days of typical sales, with limited offsetting spending elsewhere and recovery to pre-storm levels within about ten days among surviving businesses. Damage, evacuations and outages mattered more than storm category alone.
items.whatItMeans: Operational recovery models should use infrastructure damage and access restrictions, not wind-category labels alone. Transaction records omit some economic activity and may miss permanently closed businesses.
items.streamTitle: Hurricane spending losses tracked damage and outages more than storm category
items.streamSummary: Daily transaction analysis across 21 hurricanes and 7,987 ZIP codes found roughly two days of sales losses and recovery within about ten days for surviving firms. Infrastructure disruption predicted impact better than storm category.
